paper_metadata.title: CTI-Thinker: an LLM-driven system for CTI knowledge graph construction and attack reasoning
paper_metadata.abstract: The paper proposes CTI-Thinker, an LLM-driven system for constructing cyber threat intelligence knowledge graphs and performing attack reasoning. It combines in-context learning and LoRA-based fine-tuning to extract threat entities and relations, vector-based alignment for entity normalization and knowledge fusion, and a GraphRAG reasoning engine incorporating the structured graph and external ATT&CK resources. The reported experiments evaluate entity and relation extraction, alignment, and attack-oriented question answering, with claimed improvements in precision, robustness, and generalizability.

paper_metadata-authors-01-01.excerpt: Xiuzhang Yang, Ruijie Zhong, Yuling Chen, Guojun Peng, Di Yao, Chaofan Chen, Chenyang Wang, Dongni Zhang, Yilin Zhou and Zixuan Yang

paper_metadata-abstract-05-01.excerpt: We propose CTI-Thinker, a novel system that integrates large language models with semantic alignment to the ATT&CK framework for CTI knowledge graph construction and threat reasoning. First, CTI-Thinker leverages in-context learning and LoRA-based fine-tuning to extract structured threat entities and relations. Then, it adopts vector-based alignment strategies to unify heterogeneous expressions, enabling entity normalization and knowledge fusion for constructing a high-quality CTI knowledge graph.

problem_addressed: The paper addresses the conversion of heterogeneous, fragmented, and largely unstructured cyber threat intelligence reports into semantically consistent knowledge graphs that support ATT&CK-aligned attack-chain reasoning. It targets limitations of prior systems including dependence on manual annotation, isolated entity or relation extraction, weak cross-paragraph context handling, polysemy and ambiguity, fragmented entity alignment, hallucination, prompt sensitivity, and limited tactical-level inference.

methodology.description: CTI-Thinker is a four-stage LLM-based pipeline. It collects and cleans multi-source CTI, segments documents into paragraphs and sentences, and uses expert-reviewed LLM-generated annotations. A KNN retriever selects semantically similar demonstrations for in-context prompting. A LoRA-adapted LLaMA-3-8B generates standardized entity-relation triples. A two-stage alignment module first groups entities and relations by semantic category using an LLM, then applies encoder embeddings and cosine similarity with a validation-tuned threshold to merge aliases and variants. The resulting graph and summaries are indexed for GraphRAG, which retrieves relevant nodes, neighboring subgraphs, ATT&CK knowledge, and STIX 2.1 information to generate evidence-oriented tactical reasoning and question-answering responses.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: The system uses the STIX 2.1 specification for twelve entity types and produces inference results compliant with STIX 2.1 and MITRE ATT&CK standards. The relation schema contains eleven specified relation types, and ATT&CK tactic-technique mappings guide semantic alignment and reasoning.

text_to_kg_stages: Graph-based attack reasoning and question answering

input_output.input_type: Unstructured cyber threat intelligence text, including APT analysis reports, threat-event and vulnerability alerts, technical blogs, and cybersecurity consultancy material.
input_output.input_granularity: Documents are processed as paragraphs and then sentence-level units for annotation and extraction; later reasoning operates over semantically coherent document chunks, entity summaries, graph communities, and user queries.
input_output.output_representation: Standardized JSON annotations containing typed entities and relations; relational triples in the form <entity, relation, entity>; aligned and fused CTI knowledge graphs with entity summaries and graph communities; and ATT&CK/STIX-aligned reasoning answers and attack-chain representations.

models_and_tools: DeepSeek and ChatGPT for annotation prompt construction
TF-IDF similarity computation and sentence embedding encoders
datasets: Newly curated and open-sourced CTI-Thinker dataset: 2,762/345/345 train-validation-test sentences, 6,786/816/827 entities, and 3,957/477/509 relations
LLM-TIKG publicly available dataset: 1,410/176/176 train-validation-test sentences, 5,514/681/672 entities, and 2,955/374/385 relations
Real-world APT28 CTI document for qualitative extraction case study
Threat reasoning queries: 30 queries covering 20 APT organizations
APT38 and Gamaredon Group query-answering examples

metrics: F1-score for entity recognition and relation extraction
Exact-match accuracy after ontology and alias normalization for threat reasoning
Appendix reasoning score based on accuracy, completeness, and relevance
evaluation.setting: The extraction and alignment experiments use the reported CTI datasets with an 8:1:1 train-validation-test split. Models are evaluated on the same dataset under a unified evaluation framework and server environment; extraction results are averaged over ten independent runs. LoRA training uses an NVIDIA A40 48 GB GPU, maximum sequence length 1024, learning rate 2e-5, 10 epochs, gradient accumulation of 8, validation every 50 steps, checkpointing every 100 steps, and FP16. Reasoning is evaluated on 30 queries covering 20 APT organizations using exact-match accuracy and an appendix scoring rubric.

value: Entity recognition: precision 0.8314, recall 0.8458, F1 0.8385.
Relation recognition: precision 0.7769, recall 0.7610, F1 0.7689.
Compared with Bert+BiLSTM-CRF, the paper reports a 9.97% F1 improvement for entity recognition; compared with ATTCKG+ and LLM-TIKG, it reports 10.95% and 3.81% improvements, respectively.
For relation extraction, CTI-Thinker reports F1 improvements of approximately 21.26% over ATTCKG+ and 9.96% over LLM-TIKG.
KNN-based ICL with seven examples achieved triple F1 0.7689 and entity F1 0.8385; performance declined slightly at nine examples.
Alignment with SecureBERT plus embedding similarity achieved triple-alignment F1 0.7349 and entity-alignment F1 0.8288, outperforming ECBERT, CTI-BERT, and ATTACK-BERT.
At similarity threshold 0.80, the reported best threshold results were triple-alignment F1 0.7718 and entity-alignment F1 0.8383.
Reasoning accuracy over 30 queries was 0.635 for CTI-Thinker, 0.615 for LLM-RAG, and 0.223 for the Native LLM.

In qualitative examples, CTI-Thinker produced more focused, evidence-oriented answers and mapped APT38 malware and behaviors to ATT&CK techniques, while the compared non-GraphRAG outputs were described as broader, less grounded, or off-topic.
Review-level interpretation: the method covers a comparatively broad Text-to-KG workflow, combining extraction, alignment, graph construction, and graph-supported reasoning.
The paper reports strong extraction performance against the listed baselines, including entity F1 0.8385 and relation F1 0.7689.
The two-stage alignment mechanism explicitly addresses aliases, abbreviations, semantic variants, and heterogeneous expressions across CTI sources.
The GraphRAG module binds retrieval to graph entities, neighborhoods, ATT&CK mappings, and supporting evidence, improving the reported focus and traceability of answers.
The use of LoRA provides parameter-efficient adaptation of LLaMA-3-8B, while KNN-based example selection improves over random demonstration selection in the reported ICL experiments.

evidence.excerpt: The alignment results demonstrate that CTI-Thinker effectively identifies synonymous expressions, linguistic variants, and abbreviation mappings.
GraphRAG ensures factual consistency through entity linking, evidence binding, and contextual constraints, offering high-confidence support for tactical threat analysis.
CTI-Thinker consistently demonstrates superior performance across all three key metrics, achieving a precision of 0.8314, recall of 0.8458, and an F1-score of 0.8385.

value: The method remains dependent on annotated data and expert review for constructing the training corpus, despite using ICL and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
The pipeline contains multiple LLM, retrieval, alignment, and graph-indexing components, which may increase implementation and operational complexity.
The reasoning evaluation is relatively small, comprising 30 queries over 20 APT organizations, and the paper does not report a broad multilingual or cross-modal evaluation.

Review-level interpretation: reported gains are not directly comparable across unrelated datasets or task configurations; the paper's strongest claims are therefore limited to its unified experimental setting.
The paper reports residual semantic drift, redundant triples, entity aggregation errors, omission, and instability in multi-turn reasoning.

evidence.excerpt: The model is prone to semantic drift or the generation of redundant triples... These issues may lead to incorrect entity aggregation or omission.
Its ability to maintain coherent context in multi-turn reasoning scenarios... remains unstable.
The CTI-Thinker dataset is newly curated and open-sourced in this study.

value: Limited generalization in complex attack contexts with redundant expressions, heterogeneous data sources, and semantic ambiguity.
Semantic drift and redundant triples can cause incorrect entity aggregation or omission and reduce knowledge-graph completeness and downstream reasoning accuracy.
Multi-turn reasoning remains unstable, particularly for causal tracing and tactical transitions.
Reasoning-path interpretability and consistency require improvement for deployment.
The system needs stronger integration with real-world threat artifacts such as malware samples and event logs for deeper event-level reasoning and attribution.

The interpretability and consistency of reasoning paths require further improvement for deployment. Moreover, enhanced integration with real-world threat artifacts... is necessary.

value: Author-identified unresolved issues include robust generalization to ambiguous, redundant, heterogeneous, and poorly structured CTI; stable multi-turn attack-chain reasoning; interpretable and consistent reasoning paths; and event-level integration of malware and log artifacts.
Review-level inference: the paper does not establish whether the reported alignment threshold generalizes across domains, languages, or unseen entity types.
Review-level inference: hallucination control and evidence faithfulness remain dependent on retrieval, graph structure, and ontology constraints rather than being eliminated.
Review-level inference: the long-term cost, latency, maintenance requirements, and update behavior of the multi-stage system are not fully evaluated.
